name: Kanufi
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. Ninkyop [=Ninkyob, Kaninkon] wordlist paper (rogerblench.info, Ninzic directory)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Blench says Anib is 'clearly close to Ninkyob'; the sister-language wordlist may contain a tone statement that would at least characterise the subgroup. It is NOT a Kanufi description and could not supply a catalog statement for kanu1277 (identity: Ninkyob, a different Ninzic language, not Kanufi).

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. The Anib [=Kanufi] language of Central Nigeria and its affinities — any post-2011 revision with section 3.3 Tones filled in
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: The author's site is the only place a fuller version would appear; the live copy is behind a captcha (rogerblench.info-known/sgcaptcha), but the May-2025 Internet Archive copy is byte-identical to the 2011 printout, so a revision most likely does not exist. Worth one direct check or an email to the author.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2006 [printout 19 Oct 2011]. The Anib [=Kanufi] language of Central Nigeria and its affinities. Draft circulated for comment, 25 pp. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation. (= Glottolog ref 61329, listed by Glottolog as a wordlist)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Section 3 'Phonology' (printed pp. 1-2, PDF pp. 3-4) has 3.1 Vowels (eight vowels), 3.2 Consonants (table, final plosive voicing note) and a heading '3.3 Tones' whose body is empty; the words stress/accent/pitch/tonal do not occur anywhere in the text layer. Wordlist entries carry tone diacritics (e.g. Ákpúrkpòd, àrìŋkɔn, únhwɛ́) but no statement about the tone or stress system is made. The 20250524 Internet Archive copy of the same URL is byte-identical, so no later revision exists on the author's site.
Stub: 'a Plateau language of Nigeria', Kaduna State, c. 10,400 speakers (2000), Ninzic; cites only Ethnologue 18 and Glottolog. Nothing on phonology.
